title: wen xu
text:
I’m a PhD Candidate in Philosophy and Cognitive Science at the University of Colorado Boulder. My research lies at the intersection of philosophy of AI and epistemology. My dissertation develops an epistemology of LLM-mediated communication; it asks what kind of epistemic source large language models are and when, if ever, their outputs confer justification for belief. Building on this framework, my broader research agenda seeks to bring philosophical perspectives and theoretical frameworks to some central questions in AI research and policy: what trustworthy AI should mean, how to give a precise and normative account of AI hallucination, and how much information users should disclose to AI systems and under what conditions.



Adjunct Faculty, Philosophy, University of Denver (2025-)
Visiting Teaching Assistant Professor, Philosophy, University of Denver (2024-25)

title: Philosophy of AI
text:
InformationSchedule


Time: Tue & Thu 10 - 11:50 AM
Location: Sturm 333
Instructor: Wen Xu
Office Hours: Tue & Thu 8 - 9:50 AM (Sturm 263 or via Zoom)
In this course, we will explore the philosophical issues regarding our current state-of-arts generative artificial intelligence systems. Our approach is twofold: we will consider how established philosophical theories can help us make sense of the new phenomena emerging from generative AI, and, conversely, how advances in AI can inspire us to rethink, refine, and even remodel our philosophical frameworks.
The course will focus on three broad areas:

AI Metaphysics: Are current AI systems intelligent, conscious, or “minded” in any meaningful sense?
AI Epistemology: Can AI systems represent knowledge, and what can we learn from their outputs?
AI Ethics: How do AI technologies raise moral and societal concerns, including issues of fairness, justice, and social impact?

No prerequisites are required. Students should be prepared to engage in careful reading, discussion, and critical reflection on the assigned texts. 
The course follows a flipped-classroom format using a role-playing method adapted from Alec Jacobson and Colin Raffel (2021), “Role-Playing Paper-Reading Seminars.” Active and consistent participation is therefore expected.

This course is designed to introduce to you major philosophical problems and ideas. Specifically, we will focus on five topics:

Knowledge and Skepticism
Philosophy of Religion
Formal Logic
Personal Identity and Free Will
Mind and Body

Problems and issues concerning these topics have ancient roots and are widely discussed and vigorously debated among people all over the world. In this course, my goal is to lead you to explore these big ideas and to have you reflect on your own beliefs and thoughts through a philosophical lens. To achieve this goal, I will do my best to promote class discussion, intending to provoke questions and ideas in your mind. My hope is that you will come away with a deeper appreciation of what philosophy is, and why these topics are interesting.

This course is designed to introduce to you major philosophical ideas originating in ancient Greece. Specifically, we will focus on six topics from ancient philosophy: (1) Happiness, (2) Virtue, (3) Democracy, (4) Love and Friendship, (5) Fate and Freedom, and (6) Ontology. Even nowadays problems and issues concerning these topics are still widely discussed and vigorously debated among people all over the world. In this course, my goal is to lead you to explore these big ideas in historical context and to have you reflect on your own beliefs and thoughts through an ancient lens. To achieve this goal, I will do my best to promote class discussion, intending to provoke questions and ideas in your mind. My hope is that you will come away with a deeper appreciation of what philosophy is, and why the Greeks are interesting.

text:
InformationSchedule


Time: Mon & Wed, 8 - 9:50 AM
Location: Sturm 335
Instructor: Wen Xu
Office Hours: Wednesday 1 - 3 PM (via Zoom)
This course is designed to introduce to you key issues and debates within epistemology, the philosophical study of knowledge. We will explore how different epistemologists try to answer central questions such as: What is knowledge? What counts as justification? Where do knowledge and justification come from? Can we acquire them? How do we acquire them? We will also consider whether modern technology poses particular challenges to knowledge acquisition. Specifically, the course will focus on four main topics:

Justification and Knowledge
Testimony
Trust and Distrust
Thinking in the Age of AI

The goal of this course is to engage you in critical reflection on the nature and limits of human knowledge. To achieve this goal, I will do my best to promote class discussion, intending to provoke questions and ideas in your mind. My hope is that you will come away with a deeper appreciation of what epistemology is and be inspired to think critically about what it means to believe, know, and understand the world around you.

Time: Mon & Wed, 8 - 9:50 AM
Location: Sturm 312
Instructor: Wen Xu
Office Hours: Wednesday 2 - 4 PM (via Zoom)
This course offers an introduction to contemporary philosophy of language, the field that examines the nature of language and the role it plays in philosophical inquiry. We will explore how philosophers of language address questions such as: What are words, and how do they come to have meaning? How do words and phrases come to refer to things in the world? What kinds of acts do we perform in using language? The course centers on three main topics:

Formal Logic
Names and Descriptions
Communication

The goal of this course is to engage you in critical reflection on the nature and use of languages. To achieve this goal, I will do my best to promote class discussion, intending to provoke questions and ideas in your mind. My hope is that you will come away with a deeper appreciation of what language is and the role it plays in shaping how we understand the world.

title: Philosophy of Mind
text:
InformationSchedule


Time: Mon & Wed, 10 - 11:50 AM
Location: Sturm 379
Instructor: Wen Xu
Office Hours: Monday 2 - 4 PM (Sturm 263)
This course examines key questions about the nature of the mind, its relationship to the physical world, and the mechanisms underlying thought, consciousness, and behavior. Topics include foundational theories such as dualism, behaviorism, identity theory, and functionalism, as well as contemporary debates on mental causation, consciousness, and mental content. We will also explore challenges to folk psychology and the philosophical implications of artificial intelligence.
In this course, my goal is to guide you in exploring key ideas in the philosophy of mind and encourage reflection on your own beliefs. To achieve this goal, I will do my best to promote class discussion, intending to provoke questions and ideas in your mind. My hope is that you will come away with a deeper appreciation for the field and an understanding of why these topics are interesting.
